# Day 2 — Overview {#sec-day2}

Day 1 treated the data as given. The first step of the pipeline was *load and
inspect*, and `summary()` was enough: an age of 109 and a median stay of 66
days are visible to anyone who looks. Today you meet a file that does not
cooperate. Every column is numeric, nothing is marked missing, every summary
function returns a number, and more than half of one column is a clerical
convention rather than a measurement. Finding that, deciding what to do about
it, and then doing it without destroying your own evaluation is the whole day.

The thread is a single question, asked about a file rather than about a model:

> **What is wrong with this extract, and does my fix for it make my results
> better or only make them look better?**

The second half of that question is the one the day builds towards. The
pipeline table in @sec-pipeline described a held-out test set as protection
against "scoring your homework with the answers in front of you". Every
preprocessing step you write today — a mean, a median, a scaling constant, an
imputation model — is a way of copying the answers across without noticing.

## The data is synthetic, and that is worth five minutes

Days 2 to 6 use `data/diabetes.csv`: 768 adults, eight measurements, a
`pos`/`neg` outcome. These exercises were originally written against
`PimaIndiansDiabetes` — data collected from Akimel O'odham women that became
one of the most-used teaching datasets in the world. Both the UCI repository
and the `mlbench` package have since withdrawn it, because it appears to have
been included without informed consent. We use `mlbench`'s synthetic
replacement, which has the same columns, the same size and the same defects.

Copies of the original remain on third-party mirrors and nothing technical
stops anyone using them. The reason this booklet does not is that consent does
not expire because a file is convenient, and "everyone uses it" is the sentence
that kept it in circulation for thirty years. The full account, including what
`mlbench`'s own documentation says, is in @sec-data-diabetes. Read it before
Exercise 2.1, and expect to be asked in the plenary what you would have done.

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Audit an unfamiliar extract for values that are valid to the software and
  impossible in a patient, and quantify how many there are.
- Describe a missingness pattern, and say whether it is plausible as something
  a clinic produced rather than something a script did.
- Impute missing values with a stated rule and name two properties of the data
  the imputation changed.
- Say what min-max scaling, standardisation and a log transformation each
  change, and which of the three leaves the shape of a distribution untouched.
- Distinguish a preprocessing step that is *fitted* to data from one that is
  not, and explain why only the fitted ones can leak.
- Build the same pipeline leaking and leak-free, and report the difference in
  test error as a number you computed rather than a rule you were told.
:::

| | Exercise | Time | Mode |
|---|---------|------|------|
| 2.1 | [First look](day2-01-first-look.qmd) | 45 min | individual |
| 2.2 | [Missing data](day2-02-missing-data.qmd) | 45 min | individual |
| — | break | 15 min | |
| 2.3 | [Transforming](day2-03-transforming.qmd) | 40 min | individual |
| 2.4 | [Leakage](day2-04-leakage.qmd) | 60 min | individual, then pairs |
| — | [Consolidation](day2-99-consolidation.qmd) | 20 min | plenary |

: {tbl-colwidths="[6,52,18,24]"}

Do them in order. Exercise 2.4 rebuilds what it needs in its first cell, but
its argument only lands if you have personally computed the statistics in 2.2
and 2.3 from the whole file, which is the mistake it then takes apart.

## What you need before you start

- R and Python working on your laptop, and this project open in your editor
  (@sec-setup). Day 2 uses two R packages beyond the Day 1 set — `naniar` and
  `mice` — both installed by `scripts/setup_local.R`.
- Day 1's pipeline: the five steps, the split, and why a score computed on
  training rows is not evidence (@sec-pipeline).
- Nothing from Module 2 on missing data. If you have met multiple imputation
  before, you will recognise `mice` in 2.2; if you have not, you are not
  behind.

::: {.callout-note}
## What today is not
Today is about the data, not the model. Every model fitted is an ordinary
linear regression, used as a measuring instrument: it exists so that a
preprocessing choice produces a number you can compare. Choosing between
models starts on Day 3.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** The four exercises are a single argument and the last one
is the payload. 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 each end by pointing out that every statistic
computed in them came from the whole file; 2.4 then charges for it. If you are
short of time, compress 2.3 — the three transformations can be shown from the
front in ten minutes — and protect the full hour for 2.4.

**Where the time actually goes.** The zero audit in 2.1 is quick; the argument
about what the zeros did to the correlation matrix is not, and it is worth the
overrun. In 2.2, the simulation in Task 1 takes longer to explain than to run.
In 2.4, expect the room to go quiet at Leak 3 — that is the moment the day
exists for, so do not fill the silence.

**Plenary.** Ask for a show of hands on "which of the three leaks changed the
answer" before revealing anything. Most will say all three, having been taught
the rule as a ritual. The two that changed nothing are what make the third
memorable.

**The consent discussion.** Five minutes, early, and it is not optional: the
cohort will meet the original dataset in half the tutorials they find online,
and they should know why this booklet does not use it. @sec-data-diabetes has
the detail and the quotations from `mlbench`'s documentation.

**A note for the module lead.** @sec-pipeline tells students that
cross-validation arrives on Day 2, and @sec-consolidation lists resampling
first among the loose ends Day 2 picks up. This day does not teach
cross-validation — it teaches the preprocessing that has to sit inside the
resampling loop before resampling means anything. Either amend those two
pointers or say so in the Day 1 plenary.
:::
:::
